job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Iris Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up around eight in my parents' flat in Hamburg, make coffee, and sit at the desk in my old bedroom. I spend the morning on applications, mostly rewriting my cover letter for each firm because I won't send a copy-paste one. In the afternoon I practise algorithm problems by hand on paper, then walk my little brother Jonas home from school. It's been seven months since my computer science degree and I've sent about sixty applications.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of those months?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The silence, honestly. I was top of my class and did two internships, one at the city transport company and one at an insurer, so I expected calls. Most firms never reply at all, and a few send a robot-sounded rejection within an hour. My mother is a nurse and a union rep, and she keeps saying it isn't my fault, but it still stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, the hype people can calm down. At the transport company the so-called smart tools mostly produced reports nobody read. I'd tell my friends that nothing is changing and companies should just hire people again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel relieved but not safe. The job market is already stingy and rents keep climbing, so even a boring plateau isn't a happy place for someone with no offer after seven months. I know I'm lucky to have savings, but my name still isn't on any payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, about ten a week, and I'd go to the university careers fair again in spring. I'd also ask my old internship supervisor at the insurer to forward my CV inside the company. And I'd keep my savings untouched, because I want it for a deposit one day, not for rent in a flat I don't own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, like a long grey day that's at least predictable. I'm tired of waiting, but I'm not scared. If AI really stays minor, my problem is the job market, not the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the two internships teach you about routine work in your field?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the slow hiring, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you have savings and plenty of openings nearby. So what is actually worrying you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies that sit on their cash and call it caution. My mum's hospital has the same problem, with posts left empty to save money, so I see the pattern. I want rules that make firms train graduates, and a bit more public money for first jobs. Then nobody has to beg for an interview after a top degree.

say: I'd say the hype faded and firms should simply **hire** graduates again.
I'd tell friends my **seven months** of searching shows the market is the problem, not AI.
think: Privately I feel **relieved**, but one boring plateau doesn't give me an offer.
I worry that firms keep **cash** in the bank while graduates wait.
do: Send **ten applications** a week and attend the spring careers fair.
Ask my internship supervisor at the insurer to **forward** my CV inside the firm.
Leave my **savings** alone for a future deposit.
feel: **Tired** of waiting, but not scared, because the problem is the market.
S0.quote: Companies that sit on their cash and call it caution. My mum's hospital has the same problem, with posts left empty to save money, so I see the pattern.
fieldNote: She blames **employers**, not technology, and links her job hunt to her mother's hospital.
Savings give her real breathing room, yet seven months without an offer keeps her **uneasy**.
Her answer is political: training rules and public money for first jobs.

steps.text: Send ten tailored applications every week to Hamburg firms
Ask the insurer supervisor to pass my CV to hiring managers
Sign the union youth petition for funded graduate trainee posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what unions and regulation are for. If software takes over coding and checking, the gains shouldn't only go to shareholders. I'd post that firms must publish how many graduate roles they cut, and I'd say it loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared, because entry-level coding is what I trained for and what I applied to. The tasks a junior does, writing small functions and checking others' code, are the first things the tools do. I can't pretend my careful hand-written style will beat that on speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop being stubborn and try one assistant for two weeks, so I know what I'm arguing against. Then I'd widen my search to roles that need a person to sign off, like hospital systems and transport safety software. I'd also join my mother's union branch and ask about a young workers group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing on a platform where the timetable keeps changing. I'm angry more than frightened, though that may be a cover. I have six months of savings, so I won't panic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. How does that sit with this picture, where coding and checking get taken over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would tell me to hold on, as she always does. I'd say I'll try the tools to understand them, but I won't pretend I like them. I still believe a person should answer for what the software does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, and that is where my pride is. At the insurer I watched a colleague accept a machine-written fix without reading it, and it broke a payment run. I'd rather be the person who reads, but I understand that may be a narrow job.

say: I'd say firms should **publish** how many graduate roles they cut because of software.
I'd argue the gains must be shared through **unions** and rules, not just shareholders.
think: Entry-level **coding** is what I trained for, and it's exactly what the tools take first.
My hand-written style won't beat the tools on **speed**, and I know it.
do: Try one AI assistant for **two weeks** so I know what I'm arguing against.
Aim at roles that need a human **sign-off**, such as hospital and transport software.
Join my mother's **union** branch and ask about a young workers group.
feel: **Angry** more than frightened, though anger may be covering fear.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person who reads, but I understand that may be a narrow job.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** to AI tools softens: she will try one to understand it.
Her fear is specific: junior coding is the work she applied for.
She finds her footing in oversight roles and her mother's **union**.

steps.text: Test one AI coding assistant for two weeks on my own projects
Apply to hospital and transport firms that need human code reviewers
Join my mother's union branch and its young workers group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments are asleep and need to act now: income support, retraining paid for by the companies that profit, and rules that slow the roll-out. At the university I'd back the student campaign. Online I'd probably be furious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the one that frightens me. My degree is in the thing the AI does best, and the first jobs to go would be the ones I'm applying for. Two years isn't enough time even to get one year of experience on a CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to anything with a human in the loop, like safety checks, public offices, teaching computing and technical support at the hospital. I'd move into my aunt's flat in Bremen if a job appeared there. I'd also keep my six months of savings in the safest account and cut my outings to almost nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the floor tipping. I can't sleep when I think about it, and I'd lie awake counting how many months my savings last. I don't have a plan beyond holding on and pushing for rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What do you do with the first month after you hear it's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust the big AI companies at all, because they're the ones who gain. I'd trust a strong public body with real powers, like a labour regulator. Even that might be too slow for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you trust to handle this, and who don't you trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month I'd go to the union office with my mother and ask what they can do for people like me. Then I'd write to my representative. I know that sounds small, but doing nothing would feel worse than doing something small.

say: I'd say governments must act now with **income support** and retraining paid by profiting companies.
Online I'd be **furious** and back the student campaign.
think: My degree is in what AI does best, so I'd lose the jobs I'm **applying** for.
Two years is too short to build even **one year** of experience.
do: Apply to jobs with a human in the loop, like **hospital** technical support.
Move to my aunt's flat in **Bremen** if a job appeared there.
Cut outings to almost nothing and keep **savings** in the safest account.
feel: It feels like the **floor tipping**, and I'd lie awake counting my savings months.
S2.quote: My degree is in the thing the AI does best, and the first jobs to go would be the ones I'm applying for.
fieldNote: This is the first scenario where her **savings** stop feeling like enough.
She trusts public bodies and distrusts AI **companies**, in line with her outlook.
Her action is small and political: union office, then her representative.

steps.text: Apply to hospital and public office roles that need a person on duty
Write to my representative demanding paid retraining for graduates
Ask my aunt about a spare room in Bremen
Cut weekend outings and subscriptions to stretch savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something if we start now: new training, unions bargaining, rules about who is accountable. I'd tell friends to stop treating it as a private problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still be anxious, but I'd feel I have a chance. I could get a first job, build three years of experience, and be someone firms want to keep. I'm not sure that's safe, but it's a ladder, which two years doesn't give me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any decent first job, even if it's not my dream, and learn how a team really works. I'd save more, because my parents back me now but won't forever. I'd also do a part-time master's in software safety, if my employer pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit calmer, like a storm forecast I can plan around. Still heavy, though. I'd be worried for Jonas, who is nine, because his generation grows up in that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use them a bit, yes, but only the parts that help me check my work, never to write it for me. Refusing everything would just make me easier to replace. I'd rather know their weak spots, because that's where human oversight matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still refuse to use AI tools with five years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd have time to keep my mother in the loop. She wants me to be at the bargaining table, not outside it. A first job in a firm with a union would make a real difference.

say: I'd say five years is **long enough** to build training, bargaining and accountability rules.
I'd tell friends to stop treating it as a **private** problem.
think: I'd still be **anxious**, but a first job could become three years of experience.
With **five years** I get a ladder, which two years doesn't give me.
do: Take a decent **first job** even if it isn't my dream.
Save more because my parents' **backing** won't last forever.
Start a part-time master's in **software safety** if an employer pays.
feel: A bit **calmer**, like a storm forecast I can plan around, but still heavy.
S3.quote: I'd rather know their weak spots, because that's where human oversight matters.
fieldNote: Extra time moves her from **fighting** to planning.
She keeps refusing to hand writing to AI, but will use it for checking.
Worry for her brother Jonas shows her thinking beyond her own **career**.

steps.text: Accept the first reasonable graduate offer and learn the team
Move 400 euros a month into a separate savings account
Apply for a part-time master's in software safety
Ask a unionised employer about a graduate seat at the bargaining table

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do it properly. We can reform education, rebuild the unions' role and fund retraining. I'd write a long post about it for the student paper, because ten years is when change really starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly calm. By then I'd be 33, with a decade of work behind me and probably a small team to lead. The AI will take things, but ten years lets me move toward the work that needs people, like safety, auditing and care systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job within months, build up a specialty in safety-critical software, and aim for a senior role by 30. I'd also buy a small flat with a deposit rather than keep renting. And I'd learn the tools, slowly, one at a time, because ten years is long enough to be careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable, a bit like planning for a big move to another city. I'd still feel the weight of it, but it doesn't wake me at night. My relief is that I'd have time to catch up with mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years change about how you plan your life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Jonas to learn a trade that includes people, maybe nursing like my mother, or something with his hands. And I'd want him to keep a curious mind. I'd say the same to myself: a degree is not a ticket forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change what you want for your younger brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd plan a family later in that period, maybe in my late twenties, because the future would be clearer. Today I can't plan that far, but a decade gives me space for it.

say: I'd say ten years is time to **reform** education and fund retraining properly.
I'd write a long post for the **student paper** about the changes ahead.
think: I'd be fairly **calm**, because ten years lets me move toward work that needs people.
By 33 I'd have a **decade** of experience and maybe a small team.
do: Take a first job within **months** and specialise in safety-critical software.
Save a **deposit** for a small flat instead of renting forever.
Learn the AI tools one at a time, **slowly** and carefully.
feel: **Manageable**, like planning a big move to another city.
S4.quote: A degree is not a ticket forever.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her **fear** into planning, with a house deposit and a specialty.
She would still learn the tools, but on her own **terms**.
Family plans open up once the future looks readable.

steps.text: Take a first job within months and learn safety-critical code
Study for a safety-critical software certificate in evenings
Save a deposit for a small flat in Hamburg
Plan to start a family around 28 once income is steady

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because everything I trained for would be gone before I even started. What would help is public money for first jobs, rules that make firms train graduates, and a union at my side.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Being top of the class doesn't protect you. Most of what we were told about merit was a story. I'd like people to hear that graduates are scared, not lazy.

headlineQuote: Being top of the class doesn't protect you. Most of what we were told about merit was a story.
portrait: Iris is **23**, a top computer science graduate in Hamburg, living with her parents and brother.
Seven months and sixty applications have left her tired, though her **savings** keep her from panic.
She never used AI tools, but a short **trial** of one is the most she'd concede.
She blames employers and trusts unions, regulation and public **money** over companies.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, because her trained skills vanish before her career begins.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for **first jobs**, rules making firms train graduates, and a union beside her.
